claims.text: The identity of X governs the stability of the oxide layer formed on CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
CrFeCoNiAl tends to form a dual-phase oxide scale containing chromia and alumina.
A mixed chromia-alumina scale relaxes or dissipates oxide-growth and interfacial stresses.
Stress relaxation by the mixed chromia-alumina scale improves oxide adhesion at high temperature.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn form oxide scales with higher growth or interfacial stresses than CrFeCoNiAl.
The higher-stress oxide scales on the Si- and Mn-containing alloys are prone to cracking or spallation.
The alloying element X influences oxygen diffusion.
The alloying element X influences oxidation kinetics.
The alloying element X influences the development of interfacial stresses.
Si and Mn do not generate the stress-relieving oxide phase attributed to Al.
CrFeCoNiX alloys can be present as single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solutions.
The compared CrFeCoNiX samples have homogeneous and comparable microstructures.
CrFeCoNiAl will form a coherent, slow-growing, and adherent protective oxide under the specified high-temperature exposure.
CrFeCoNiSi and CrFeCoNiMn will crack or spall more than CrFeCoNiAl under identical exposure conditions.
A CrFeCoNi alloy lacking X, or containing only a minimal amount of X, can serve as the baseline for isolating the effect of X.
The proposed behavior applies at or above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments for durations sufficient to produce observable oxide scales.
The three X variants are to be compared under a common oxidative exposure of 950 °C for about 100 hours.
Comparable oxide stability in the Si- or Mn-containing alloys, or failure of the Al-containing alloy to show superior coherence and adhesion, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
